projects.title: AgriField
projects.description: Built AgriShield at the United Nations x San Diego Supercomputer Center Reboot the Earth hackathon — a farm-level wildfire planning tool that helps farmers prepare before fire season begins.AgriShield lets users draw a farm parcel, map crops and key assets, overlay wildfire risk factors, and generate recommendations for firebreaks, low-fuel buffers, water points, and access routes across three protection tiers. The tool is designed to reduce wildfire exposure while preserving the farmer’s preferred crop layout as much as possible.Built with Python and ELMFIRE for fire-spread simulation, with a focus on turning wildfire risk maps into practical, farm-specific planning decisions.

activity.title: Open weight models are supposed to close the gap with the frontier labs. And the weights really are open. The alignment is not. Nobody ships a list of what a model was post-trained to refuse. So you find it the way I did. I built a bot that writes my morning news brief. 130 headlines in, a 60,000 character PDF out. Last week it delivered one empty page. I assumed auth, because it had been auth before. It wasn't. HTTP 200, valid response, 13 characters of Chinese saying it could not provide the content. finish_reason=content_filter. DeepSeek had not failed. It had declined. So I tested it: take a bundle it writes happily, inject one suspect headline, repeat. "India Names 27 Places in Arunachal Pradesh | Counters China's Renaming Claims" With that headline, 8 of 12 calls refused. Without it, 0 of 12. Then I went looking for the boundary and could not find it. A Taiwan tensions headline from the same feed: 0 of 8. A written-to-order headline of Taiwan's president declaring the island sovereign and rejecting Beijing's claim: 0 of 3. The same Arunachal sentence with China swapped for Britain and the Falklands: 0 of 3. Not the topic. Not the region. Not the framing. That one story. Open weight feels like control. Download it, self host it, switch providers, no vendor policy layer in the way. All true of the infrastructure. None of it true of the model. No setting, no policy page, no support ticket, and switching providers changes nothing, because it was never the provider's rule. You are not just picking a model. You are picking whose regulatory environment decided what it will write about. In a chat window you would never notice. In an automated pipeline it is an empty page at 8am. Two thirds of the time, for one headline out of 130. ...more

I moved to the Bay Area with one goal: do more hackathons. So I checked Luma about as often as I checked Instagram. Then Cerebral Valley. Then whatever else I could find. And I still kept hearing about hackathons the same way every time, from someone at another event, mentioning one that had already happened, that had never appeared anywhere I looked. The frustrating part is that Luma is ideally supposed to solve this. Follow enough calendars, attend enough events, and discovery is meant to come to you. I'd signed up for around 15 tech events in a span of 20 days. My feed was still missing hackathons I would have definitely gone to. So I built my own calendar just for fun. Some GitHub Actions, some scraping, and a classifier that decides what actually counts as a hackathon, it reads 9+ independent sources twice a day, including the curated boards themselves, and publishes one calendar you subscribe to once and then forget about. It currently lists 23 upcoming Bay Area hackathons. The best-known Luma hackathon calendar lists 9 (one of which is a pitch competition). Subscribe here: luma.com/hacklist-sf , the site and the calendar feed are both linked from there. And if you find a Bay Area hackathon it missed, genuinely tell me. That's the most useful thing you could send me right now. I only did this for SF and the bay right now because that's where I am. But nothing about it is SF-specific, if this turns out to be useful to even one of you, tell me which hackathon-dense city you want next and I'll get one out. ...more

2 for 2, that was quick. We came first at the Voice Coding Hackathon hosted by Voice Cursor , Convex and Respan . Everyone built around daily logistics and tasks. We went a level higher and built for search and rescue, but as assistance rather than the primary driver, because when someone's missing the searchers already know what they're doing, they just don't know where to look first. That's the actual bottleneck. LOCUS takes a last known point and a pile of unreliable tips, runs a Monte Carlo sim of hundreds of simulated lost persons walking outward using real lost-person behavior models, and turns where they pile up into a live probability heatmap the coordinator drives entirely by voice. The entire backend was basically on Convex and it held up better than anything I've shipped in a day. Thanks to Henry Song , Wayne Sutton and all the other hosts for running it. Built with Dat , Pranav and Mohak . github: https://lnkd.in/gkbJqRVN ...more

The SF hackathon run is off to a good start. We took 1st place at the Loop Engineering Hackathon hosted by tokens& at the AWS Builder Loft (best hackathon venue i've been to yet). 250 people, 100 projects, one afternoon to build something worth winning. The idea started simple but got sharper as we went. We built Vigil: an AI on-call engineer that detects, diagnoses, and rolls back production incidents while holding zero standing credentials. Every other agent demo right now is a race to hand the model everything, more keys, more access, more scope, so we inverted that. Vigil holds nothing at rest. Every destructive action gets a single-use credential scoped to one service, expiring in literally 60 seconds. Zero sells it a log parser per call, Overclock Labs, creators of Akash Network runs a disposable sandbox that reproduces the failure before anything touches production (which won us best use), Pomerium gates every rollback against policy, and OpenAI adds a root-cause hypothesis on top. When Vigil later tried a mass-restart across 12 services, the gate denied it. That denial is the whole thesis. The model never gets trusted, it gets contained. That's least-privilege for autonomous agents, shown end to end. Shoutout to Dat and Pranav and their Claude max subscriptions. feat. drippiest duck in sf ...more

I can’t remember the last time I lost. Genuinely. I’ve tried. It’s not in there. Berkeley. Bow Capital. MLH x DigitalOcean. And this weekend, 1st in the Akash track at the Loop Engineering Hackathon, inside the AWS Builder Loft. 4 for 4. At some point “lucky” stops being the word. We built Vigil, an autonomous on-call engineer that fixes production incidents on its own and never holds the keys to prod. Moved to Mountain View this summer as a GTM Engineer intern at GMI Cloud and I've been learning way more than what I anticipated. The thing about working at a cloud infra company is you don't just drive growth, but you live the product. You start to understand which models actually deliver, which ones overpromise, and why the model you pick is only half the decision. GMI posted something this week that stuck with me: instead of relying on one frontier model, you run Opus 4.8 first and let GLM 5.2 clean up what it misses. 94/100 pass rate, 47% cheaper than Fable 5. The combo outperformed every individual model on both cost and accuracy. That's the kind of insight you only get when you're close to the infra layer, seeing what's actually out there beyond the names everyone defaults to. The work culture here is something I didn't know I needed. Slim team, everyone has agency, everyone owns what they do. High energy, no fluff and I decided this is the kind of environment I want to keep working in. I'll be coming down to SF most weekends for hackathons and Luma events, so hmu if you want to do a hackathon together or just chat. Also just made an X, apparently that's the new LinkedIn. Come find me at https://x.com/Lgoyal6 ...more

We’ve raised $500K from a16z speedrun ! It’s crazy I finally get to share this. I’ve wanted to write that sentence since I was 10. I used to binge-watch Shark Tank, keep a list with hundreds of startup ideas, and doodle future logos in my school notebooks. Then I moved to the US to study at UIUC, and things started feeling real. I met Ansh , we boiled ramen in his kettle together, and started building things that fascinated us. (Completely ruined the kettle btw.) Somewhere between campus pitches, hackathons, and a lot of questionable product ideas, I got incredibly lucky with mentors who kept taking my ideas seriously long before they deserved to be. Andrew D'Souza and the Boardy team took a bet on me. They gave me my first real glimpse of what it looks like when people are completely obsessed with something they’re building. I wanted that for myself. Ansh and I built our first prototype for ChatOverflow in February. Four weeks later, we were backed by a16z speedrun. A huge thank you to my friends who tolerated my worst startup ideas at 2am before a final; to my teachers who believed in me really early on; and to my family, who have always supported me, forever smiling (sometimes nervously), even through the occasional “maybe I should drop out” conversations : ) Now loving every moment of speedrun with Fareed Mosavat , Andrew Chen , Jonathan Lai , Troy Kirwin , Joan DeGennaro , Samira Behrouzan , Tabish Gilani , Macy Mills , Jordan Mazer , Jordan Carver , Lester Chen , Tom Hammer , and so many more. You guys make speedrun ridiculously fun. Back to building! 🚀

At 15, I installed 770 solar panels in Khapa, a village outside Nagpur with fifteen power cuts a day. The technology had existed for decades. It had just never arrived. That's still the whole problem: frontier tech doesn't die in the lab. It dies in the last mile. So that's my business. Companies pay me to deploy them into India's factories, schools, and hospitals. If the deployment works, I invest. It inverts deal flow. The best companies come to me because they need the road. And I've seen them execute with real customers before I put in a dollar. Other investors read memos. I've seen the machine run. Thanks Dave McClure for pressure-testing this pitch until it said what I meant. The technology was never the hard part. Arriving is.

FORWARD DEPLOYED ENGINEER. Yes, that's my new title. And no, my mother still doesn't know what I do. So here's what I actually do as an FDE at Hyperscience I'm the engineer who goes to the customer. Not the deck version of their workflow. The real one. Half the job is engineering. The other half: → Translator → Detective → Bad news deliverer → Occasionally, therapist My favorite part is the moment someone says "oh, we also do this other thing" on day four. That sentence has cost me more sleep than any deadline. But that's the job. The model isn't the hard part anymore. Surviving contact with a real business is. Every company shipping AI is hitting that wall right now. Which is why this role went from nonexistent to everywhere in two years. Been doing the work for years. Glad it finally has a name. If you're an engineer curious about this kind of work, my DMs are open! #ForwardDeployedEngineer #AIEngineering #EnterpriseAI #SoftwareEngineering #AIinProduction

The reality in today's market: a startup offering $300-350K base plus "paper money" (equity that hasn't proven itself yet) is not going to attract top talent. Unless you have a genuinely killer product and a promising future, that comp just doesn't cut it anymore. I'm talking about your average, healthy growth startup here, not the handful of outliers everyone already knows about. So you've got a few real options. Look for talent outside the Bay Area. Stop expecting every candidate to come from Stanford, Berkeley, and the usual handful of schools. Or start offering $500K cash. You can't have it both ways.
